title: How can art tell a story?
essentialQuestion: How can images and objects carry a message?
learningGoal: Use details you can see in an artwork to support an interpretation, and accept that other interpretations may be possible.

warmUp.question: When you look at a picture, what do you notice first?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: What can you see in the poster before you decide what it means?

sources.caption: What you can see in the poster
details: A blue river runs through the centre.
Three people carry buckets towards one water tap.
A child points at a cracked pipe.
The words “Water for every street” are at the bottom.

cases.name: Viewer 1
cases.body: “I think the poster is about people who do not have enough water.”

cases.name: Viewer 2
cases.body: “I think the poster asks the town to fix the broken pipe.”

sections.heading: Start with what you can see
sections.text: When you look at an artwork, begin with what you can see. Name the colours, people, objects and any words. Notice the composition, which means how the parts are arranged. In the poster, a blue river runs through the centre. Three people carry buckets towards one tap, and a child points at a cracked pipe. These are observations. They are facts that anyone can check by looking. The words “Water for every street” are also part of the evidence. Only after you look closely should you decide what the artwork might mean.
sections.simpler: First, look at what you can see. Name the colours, people, things and words. See how the parts are placed. This is the composition. A blue river is in the middle. Three people carry buckets to one tap. A child points at a broken pipe. These are observations. Anyone can check them by looking. The words on the poster are evidence too. Look closely first. Then think about what it means.

sections.heading: Art has told stories for a very long time
sections.text: People around the world use art to tell stories and keep knowledge. At Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria, rock art shows hippos and herds of cattle. The land there is desert today, so the pictures tell us the Sahara was once much greener. In China, there is a painted scroll more than five metres long. It shows over 800 people shopping, travelling and working in a busy city about 900 years ago. It is called Along the River During the Qingming Festival. In Vanuatu, in the Pacific, sand drawers use one finger to draw one long line. Their drawings help people remember stories and knowledge.
sections.simpler: People all over the world tell stories with art. In Algeria, old rock art shows cows and river animals. Now the land is desert. So the art tells us the land was once green. In China, a long painted scroll shows a busy city. It shows more than 800 people. They shop, work and travel. In Vanuatu, people draw in the sand with one finger. The drawings help them remember stories.

sections.heading: Build an interpretation with evidence
sections.text: An interpretation is an idea about what an artwork means. A strong interpretation points to details. Viewer 1 thinks the poster is about people who do not have enough water. The line of people at one tap and the words at the bottom support this idea. Viewer 2 thinks the poster asks the town to fix the pipe, because the child points right at it. Both ideas use evidence, so both can make sense. It also helps to think about the audience, the people the artist wanted to reach. Words like “may” and “might” show that you are being careful.
sections.simpler: An interpretation is an idea about what art means. A good one points to details. Viewer 1 thinks some people do not have enough water. Many people wait at one tap. That is a clue. Viewer 2 thinks the poster asks the town to fix the pipe. The child points at it. Both ideas use evidence. Think about the audience too. Who did the artist want to reach? Use words like “may” and “might”.

glossary.definition: The way the parts of a picture are placed.
glossary.example: In the poster's composition, the river runs through the centre.

glossary.definition: Something you notice by looking, which others can check.
glossary.example: “A child points at a cracked pipe” is an observation.

glossary.definition: A long roll of paper or cloth with pictures or writing.
glossary.example: The painted scroll from China shows more than 800 people.

glossary.definition: An idea about what something means, based on clues.
glossary.example: Saying the poster is about fixing the pipe is one interpretation.

glossary.definition: The people an artist or writer wants to reach.
glossary.example: The poster's audience may be the people who run the town.

checks.question: Which of these is an observation?

options.text: A child points at a cracked pipe.
options.feedback: Yes. You can see the child pointing at the pipe. Anyone can check it by looking.

options.text: The artist is angry with the town.
options.feedback: Not quite. We cannot see the artist's feelings. That is a guess. Look for something you can see.

options.text: Every street in the town is dry.
options.feedback: Not quite. The poster does not show every street. Look for something you can see.

checks.question: What does the rock art at Tassili n'Ajjer tell us?

options.text: The desert has always been dry and empty.
options.feedback: Not quite. The rock art shows hippos and cattle, and they need water and grass.

options.text: The Sahara was once much greener.
options.feedback: Yes. Hippos and cattle need water and grass, so the land was once much greener.

options.text: People there never kept any animals.
options.feedback: Not quite. The rock art shows herds of cattle. Look again at the part about rock art.

checks.question: What new facts about the poster could change your interpretation?
checks.placeholder: Think about who made it, where it was shown, and who it was for ...

write.prompt: Write a short caption for the poster. Name two details you can see, say what the poster may mean, and explain why.
selfCheck: I described two details I can see.
I gave one interpretation using “may” or “might”.
I said which details support my idea.
write.example: The poster shows three people carrying buckets to one water tap. I can also see a child pointing at a cracked pipe. This may suggest that some streets do not have enough water. I think this because many people share one tap, and the words say “Water for every street”. Another viewer might think the poster asks the town to fix the pipe. Both ideas use details from the poster.

speak.partnerTask: One person describes the poster for 20 seconds without saying what it means. The other gives an interpretation and one detail that supports it.
speak.independentTask: Choose one detail from the poster, or from an artwork in the lesson. Say what it may suggest.

watch.title: How Are Everyday Things Made Special?
watch.channel: Ayala Museum, ATIN: Stories from the Collection
watch.why: This is the Lesson 15 video again; this time, watch for the details that help objects tell a story.
watch.beforeQuestion: What is the difference between describing an object and saying what it means?
watch.afterQuestion: Which questions help you learn from an object without making up its meaning?
watch.summary: This is the same short video from Lesson 15. It comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. This time, watch closely for details. The video shows a small green pot from China with two dragons on it. It shows a salakot, a wide woven hat, decorated with shell and silver. It also shows a small cloth with a poem sewn into it. Each detail is a clue. The dragons make the pot unusual, because most pots like it were plain. The shell and silver suggest that an important person owned the hat. The poem tells us how the cloth's owner felt. A careful viewer first says what they see. Then they say what it might mean, and which details support that idea.
keyPoints: Start with details you can see.
Link the details to a possible meaning.
A good interpretation explains its evidence and stays open to other ideas.

visual.description: The fictional poster from the evidence, drawn as a simple, bright poster: a blue river through the centre, three people carrying buckets towards one water tap, a child pointing at a cracked pipe, and the words “Water for every street” along the bottom. Small numbered tags (1 to 4) mark each detail so learners can refer to them in their answers.

educatorNotes: The poster is about water, which may connect to hard experiences for some learners. Keep the focus on reading the picture, and let learners choose the lesson's other artworks if they prefer.
Model the difference between “I see ...” (observation) and “I think ... because ...” (interpretation). Learners often mix the two at first.
You could add a local mural, poster or painted sign, or show pictures of the Tassili n'Ajjer rock art or the Qingming scroll, which are easy to find on museum websites.
changes: Expanded the reading from about 80 to about 290 words, adding a new section with real examples of art that tells stories from Africa (Tassili n'Ajjer, Algeria), Asia (the Qingming scroll, China) and the Pacific (Vanuatu sand drawings).
Added two fictional viewers to the evidence so learners can compare interpretations, and rewrote simpler English at a much lower level.
Added a warm-up, self-check and visual plan; fixed glossary words that never appeared in the text.
Moved the second correct answer out of the first position and rewrote all feedback.
